title: The 1:34 a.m. Email That Ended Zirtual and More Than 400 Jobs
dek: In August 2015 a funding round collapsed days before payroll, and Maren Kate Donovan told Zirtual's assistants overnight that their jobs had already ended.

story.event: Laying off about 400 staff by overnight email after a funding round collapsed
story.summary: In the early hours of 10 August 2015 Zirtual, a virtual-assistant start-up founded by Maren Kate Donovan in 2011, told its roughly 400 staff by email that it had ceased operations and their employment had ended the previous Friday. Donovan said costs had soared after the company turned contractors into employees and a last-minute funding round collapsed; staff were paid for time worked and Startups.co bought the company within days.
paragraphs: At 1:34 in the morning on Monday 10 August 2015, Maren Kate Donovan, chief executive of Zirtual, emailed her staff. "Effective immediately, Zirtual will cease all operations," it said; their last day of employment had been the previous Friday. More than 400 people, most of them full-time employees working remotely across the United States, lost their jobs. Some read it on their phones as they woke for work.

Donovan had started Zirtual in 2011, at 25, matching entrepreneurs with virtual assistants. Early in 2015, with revenue near $1 million a month, it moved its contractors onto the payroll with health insurance, paid holiday and a retirement plan. She later wrote that costs "skyrocketed". Her accounts of what she knew differ: that week she told the Las Vegas Sun the trouble was discovered only the Monday before; about two years later she said she had suspected errors in the company's projections that spring.

By her later account, she asked investors for money to tide the company over, and some agreed. In early August, as the round was about to close, one investor pulled back and the others followed, leaving four days before a payroll the company could not meet. She and her co-founders spent the weekend making calls. Explaining the lack of notice, she wrote that she had tried to raise money "up until the 11th hour", and that once the next payroll was clearly out of reach, the law required them to terminate everyone.

Two days after the email she published an account on Medium. Zirtual had raised almost $5 million and had nearly 500 staff at its peak. "I cry for all the employees we hurt," she wrote. Everyone, she said, would be paid in full for time worked; she later said doing so emptied the bank account. She also told the Sun she blamed herself for not hiring senior finance and operations people a year earlier.

Startups.co, whose chief executive Wil Schroter was a Zirtual client, bought the company and planned to restart it with a small number of assistants. Donovan stepped down, and she and her co-founders spent months, she said, finding jobs and referrals for former staff. Looking back, she wrote: "I should have rang the alarm bell earlier."

quote.text: Words causing no man woe, words ever true, Gentle and pleasing words
quote.locator: Chapter XVII, "The Book of Religion by the Threefold Kinds of Faith" (verse 15 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: The Gita asks that speech be true and cause no one woe. In August 2015 Donovan could not offer both: the silence while she chased money spared her staff worry and cost them notice, and the true email, when it came at last, could not be gentle.

reflection: Most of the people who opened that email were not founders or investors. Donovan herself later said most were mothers working from home, with bills that would not wait for the next round. Whatever else the story teaches, it is a reminder of how far a single night's decision can travel into other people's kitchens.

You will rarely face anything this large. But smaller versions come: a project slipping, a month that will be tight, a promise you may not keep. The pull is to wait until you know for certain, hoping the news will soften. Sometimes it does. Often the waiting only means that when the truth arrives, it arrives all at once.
invitation: If you are holding a piece of unwelcome news until it is certain, tell one person it affects the plain version today, while they still have time to plan around it.

cross_checks.claim: Zirtual's staff were told by email in the early hours of 10 August 2015 that it had ceased operations, effective the previous Friday
About 400 (reported as 'more than 400') employees lost their jobs
Donovan attributed the collapse to costs that soared after contractors became employees, and to failing to raise more money
Startups.co, led by Wil Schroter, bought Zirtual within days and planned to restart it

research_notes: Timing of the email: Las Vegas Weekly gives 1:34 a.m. on 10 August 2015; an employee told Tech.co it arrived at 4:30 a.m., which matches 1:34 a.m. Pacific seen from the East Coast; Donovan's later account in The Hustle says midnight on Sunday 9 August. The story uses the contemporary 1:34 a.m. on Monday 10 August. Headcount: Entrepreneur says about 400, Las Vegas Weekly 400-plus, the Las Vegas Sun and Fortune more than 400; Donovan's Medium post says almost 500 at the company's peak. The story says more than 400 lost their jobs and gives her 'nearly 500' only as the peak. Funding: Donovan's Medium post and Fortune say almost $5 million over three years; The Hustle (her retrospective) says about $5 million from about 20 investors over five years; the Las Vegas Sun says more than $3.2 million had come in since June, which appears to count recent bridge or debt money. The story uses 'almost $5 million', her contemporary figure. What she knew and when: in a text to the Las Vegas Sun that week she said the difficulties were discovered only the Monday before; in the later as-told-to account she said she suspected errors in the projections that spring. Both are given in the story. The Hustle piece is dated 1 October 2024 on its current site but says 'looking back 2 years later', so it was evidently first written around 2017; the story says 'about two years later'. Blame: the story gives only Donovan's own explanations (burn after reclassifying workers, failing to raise money, not hiring senior finance staff sooner, not raising the alarm earlier). It does not repeat an investor's public criticism of the board and management, nor reports that law firms were looking into whether federal 60-day notice rules applied, because no ruling or finding was found. Pay: Donovan's Medium post says everyone would be compensated fully for time worked, with PTO and refunded benefit charges; The Hustle says paying them emptied the account; no independent confirmation of payment was found, so the story attributes both to her. Her Medium post is blocked for the verifier and is cited from the Internet Archive's September 2015 copy. 'Rang' is as printed in The Hustle.
